plot_extraction.response_text:
Detective Philo Gubb uses reward money from a previous case to reduce the large debt keeping him from marrying Syrilla, who remains trapped as an overweight sideshow performer. Meanwhile, Riverbank residents report bizarre “un-burglaries”: someone enters their homes, leaves engraved silver spoons, and escapes through cellar windows. Town joker Billy Getz and Marshal Wittaker encourage Gubb to investigate, expecting his amateur methods to make him look foolish.

Gubb initially suspects Billy, but stains from a flower bed lead him to wealthy, miserly John Westcote. Believing Westcote may be secretly making amends for wedding gifts he never gave, Gubb follows him. Westcote drops a package near a lumberyard, where hidden men retrieve it. Gubb trails them to a railway boxcar and overhears that they are dynamiters who have extorted one thousand dollars from Westcote and plan further violence. He locks them inside the car and accompanies the train until authorities can arrest them; their confession implicates three accomplices.

Back in Riverbank, the police catch the actual un-burglar, a harmless half-wit who dreamed that giving silverware to prominent families would earn him invitations to their parties. Thus, while the others expected Gubb to fail comically, he inadvertently solves the more serious dynamiting case and earns a share of a five-thousand-dollar reward.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the style of an early twentieth-century comic detective tale, combining small-town realism, farce, verbal misunderstanding, and an accidentally successful mystery plot. Its central method is sustained incongruity: Philo Gubb appears foolish, speaks in malapropisms, and relies on correspondence-school formulas, yet his eccentric reasoning repeatedly brings him into contact with genuine crime. The narrative treats him with amused irony but not contempt. His vanity and limited education are comic, while his persistence, suspicion, and practical resourcefulness make him more capable than the supposedly sensible people around him.

The narrator is third-person omniscient, moving freely between Gubb, Marshal Wittaker, Billy Getz, and other townspeople. The voice is clear, brisk, and outwardly matter-of-fact, often reporting absurd events as if they were entirely logical. This deadpan presentation intensifies the humor, particularly in explanations of “un-burglary” and in Gubb’s distinction between “retail” and “wholesale” detecting. The narrator occasionally enters Gubb’s thought process in free indirect style, allowing his bizarre deductions to unfold with apparent seriousness: wedding presents, guilty conscience, and senile restitution become a plausible chain because the prose temporarily accepts his premises.

The diction mixes standard narrative English with strongly individualized colloquial speech. Gubb’s dialogue is marked by rural or nonstandard grammar—“them shares,” “I ain’t no expert,” “he done it”—and by comic professional jargon such as “deteckative,” “deteckating,” “induc-i-tively,” and “docket.” His speech repeatedly inflates simple ideas into clumsy abstractions, as in “the indebtedness of the liability I now owe you.” This contrast between grand terminology and imperfect understanding is one of the story’s main comic signatures. Other characters have similarly recognizable verbal patterns: Millbrook’s agitated remarks repeatedly “gurgle”; Wittaker speaks in relaxed small-town idiom; Billy Getz uses quick, teasing banter; and Frank the Tailor is represented through exaggerated phonetic dialect. The latter reflects period conventions of ethnic caricature and would read as conspicuously stereotyped to a modern audience.

Dialogue dominates the story and performs several functions at once. It supplies exposition, differentiates characters, generates jokes, and advances the mystery. Exchanges often operate through repetition, correction, or literal-minded extension. Medderbrook solemnly corrects “Perfectly Worthless” to “Utterly Hopeless”; Wittaker and Griscom debate whether a window was broken “into” or “out of”; and Gubb builds an elaborate theory from the grammatical possibility that if one can “burgle,” one can also “un-burgle.” Comic timing depends on short replies, interruptions, delayed corrections, and speakers accidentally revealing more than they intend. Billy’s line, “Oh, you won’t catch—I mean, we will leave that to you,” is characteristic: the near-slip alerts both Gubb and the reader to the prank while preserving the scene’s playful surface.

The syntax is generally straightforward and chronological, with longer sentences reserved for explanations, deductions, or enumerated physical action. Repetition supplies rhythm, especially in dialogue and parallel constructions: a man can “tie” and “un-tie,” “hitch” and “un-hitch,” therefore “burgle” and “un-burgle.” Such sequences mimic formal reasoning while exposing its absurdity. Parenthetical clarifications and appositions establish the provincial scale of Riverbank, as when the marshal is explained as the equivalent of a chief of police “in a larger city.” Exclamation points, rhetorical questions, and repeated words convey theatrical agitation without requiring psychological depth.

The humor is primarily verbal, situational, and structural. Verbal comedy arises from malapropisms, dialect, invented compounds, pedantic corrections, and over-literal reasoning. Situational comedy appears in the reversed burglary, the flour-shooting “lung-tester,” the detective carrying false beards to an ordinary meeting, and several men independently staining their trousers by falling into flower beds. Structural comedy comes from dramatic irony: Billy and Wittaker think they are manipulating Gubb, Gubb believes Billy is the culprit, and all of them overlook the separate, genuine criminal plot that Gubb discovers while pursuing the wrong theory. The story’s deepest joke is that erroneous reasoning produces a correct and valuable result.

The plot is episodic but tightly linked by recurring clues and motifs. It begins with financial and romantic continuity from an earlier adventure, shifts into the self-contained un-burglary mystery, and ends by reconnecting Gubb with the dynamiters mentioned in the opening sentence. This creates a circular construction: the case that previously failed is solved incidentally through a different investigation. Apparent clues are frequently misread or reassigned. The chicken bone seems worthless, the pansy stains appear incriminating, and Westcote’s bundle suggests wedding restitution; in reality, these details belong to overlapping stories involving a harmless un-burglar, a blackmail payment, and the dynamiters. The convergence is deliberately improbable, fitting the farcical rather than strictly puzzle-based mode.

Pacing alternates between leisurely comic conversations and rapid nocturnal action. The first half spends substantial time establishing the joke and allowing characters to debate its logic. Once Gubb shadows Westcote, the prose becomes more visual and kinetic: movement through hazel brush, streets, lumber piles, railway yards, and boxcars is described in quick succession. The climax is notably economical. Gubb overhears enough to identify the criminals, locks them in the car, and is carried away on the train; the mechanics of his later success are compressed into a telegram. This abrupt reporting preserves the comic emphasis on the townspeople’s embarrassment rather than turning the ending into a conventional action sequence.

Characterization is caricatural but efficient. Each figure is built around a dominant trait: Medderbrook is miserly, Billy mischievous, Wittaker complacent, Millbrook excitable, Westcote notoriously mean, and Gubb solemnly self-important. Physical tags reinforce these traits, such as Gubb’s lankness, Millbrook’s short stout body and husky gurgling voice, and Westcote’s tottering gait and poor eyesight. Emotional complexity is limited, but Gubb receives a measure of sympathy through his love for Syrilla, his financial obligation, and his genuine concern that the un-burglar may be ruining himself. These touches prevent him from becoming merely a fool.

The setting is a compact, socially interconnected American town in which everyone knows the local joker, household finances, dinner habits, and personal reputations. Specific street names, businesses, municipal rooms, railway sidings, newspaper-wrapped bundles, telegrams, and shop signs create a concrete period atmosphere. The town functions almost like a stage set: the same citizens, jokes, rumors, and clues circulate rapidly across a small number of recognizable locations. Modern technologies of the period—the telephone, telegram, railway, and correspondence course—are treated as ordinary but also supply comic possibilities.

The story repeatedly parodies detective-fiction conventions. Gubb invokes Sherlock Holmes, “inductive” reasoning, shadowing rules, disguises, notebooks, reports, and professional badges, but applies them mechanically or incorrectly. The Rising Sun correspondence school represents packaged expertise: Gubb has absorbed the gestures and vocabulary of detection without mastering its principles. Yet the parody remains double-edged, because formal authorities fare no better. Wittaker dismisses the mystery as a joke, Purcell catches only the harmless culprit, and Billy’s superior amusement collapses when Gubb secures the dynamiters and their reward. The narrative therefore mocks both amateur pretension and official complacency.

The ending uses reversal and understatement rather than celebration. Gubb’s triumph arrives indirectly in the sheriff’s terse telegram, while the final lines remain with Wittaker and Billy, who confess disgust and “bilious” embarrassment. This preserves the story’s comic tone and makes social humiliation, rather than criminal capture, the true punch line. Overall, the style is genial, fast-moving, dialogue-heavy, and elaborately ironic: a burlesque of logical detection in which linguistic confusion, coincidence, and stubborn literalism repeatedly outperform conventional intelligence.

## PHILO GUBB AND THE UN-BURGLAR

When Philo Gubb received the reward for solving the celebrated case of the Missing Municipal Mule, he did not squander it.

He paid all but three hundred and sixteen dollars and forty cents of it to Syrilla’s employer.

This left only seven hundred and eighty-three dollars and sixty cents between Syrilla and freedom, because Syrilla was still known professionally as Princess Serephina, the Magnificent Mountain of Mesopotamia, and her contract with Professor Bologni’s United Wonders required her to remain a Magnificent Mountain until the money advanced for her costumes, meals, lithographs, and enlarged platform had been repaid.

Syrilla was not Mesopotamian and she was not a princess. She had been born in Keokuk, and her true ambition was to become Mrs. Philo Gubb and keep chickens behind a neat white cottage. Unfortunately, she weighed six hundred and eight pounds at the last public weighing, and Professor Bologni considered her too valuable to surrender for sentimental reasons.

Philo visited her whenever the United Wonders exhibited within reasonable railway distance of Riverbank.

“Seven hundred and eighty-three dollars and sixty cents,” he told her on his latest visit. “That is all which intervenes between us and the matrimonial altar.”

“It sounds like plenty,” said Syrilla.

“It is plenty when considered as an indebtedness,” Philo admitted, “but it is trifling when viewed as a reward.”

He was thinking of the five-thousand-dollar reward offered for the capture of the men who had dynamited the stone crusher outside Derlingport. Philo had previously made an effort to capture those men. The effort had not been successful. He had captured two umbrella menders, a Methodist Sunday-school superintendent, and a traveling salesman selling a cough cure, but none of them had dynamited anything.

“That five thousand would set us up handsome,” Syrilla said.

“It would,” Philo agreed. “And it is my fixed deteckative intention to acquire it, if the criminals will kindly remain uncaptured until I can locate their whereabouts.”

He kissed the tips of Syrilla’s fingers through the bars that separated the public from the platform. The bars were advertised as necessary because of Princess Serephina’s savage Oriental disposition, although they were chiefly useful in preventing boys from crawling under the platform to see how it was built.

When Philo returned to Riverbank, he resumed his paper-hanging business and his study of Lesson Eleven of the Rising Sun Correspondence School of Detecting. Lesson Eleven was entitled “Shadowing a Suspect Without Appearing to Do So.” It advised the student to carry three false mustaches, two reversible coats, blue spectacles, a limp, and a daily newspaper.

Philo had the newspaper and the limp. The limp was not strictly false, because he had stepped off the train onto a milk can.

He had studied half the lesson when Marshal Wittaker came into his shop.

The marshal of Riverbank performed the duties that would have been performed by a chief of police in a larger city. He also collected the dog tax and rang the fire bell when the bell ringer was at dinner.

“Gubb,” he said, “we’ve got a crime for you.”

Philo placed one long finger between the pages of his lesson.

“Retail or wholesale?” he asked.

“What?”

“Detecting,” Philo explained. “A retail deteckative matter is when one criminal commits one crime against one party. A wholesale matter is when numerous criminals commit numerous crimes against the public in general, such as dynamiting, counterfeiting, or putting crooked bottoms in berry boxes.”

“This is burglarizing,” said Wittaker.

“Retail,” Philo decided.

“Except nobody took anything.”

Philo frowned.

“A burglar entered a residence and did not take anything?”

“He left something.”

Philo closed his lesson.

“That,” he said, “is wholesale peculiar.”

Marshal Wittaker seated himself on a roll of wallpaper and told the circumstances. During the night someone had entered the home of Mr. and Mrs. Amos Griscom through a cellar window. Nothing in the house had been disturbed, but in the morning Mrs. Griscom had found a silver spoon lying on the parlor table. It was a handsome spoon, with a twisted handle, and on it were engraved the words:

TO AMOS AND AMELIA  
WITH ESTEEM

“Was the cellar window broke into?” Philo asked.

“Griscom says it was broke out of.”

“A window can’t be broke out of by a man getting in.”

“That’s what I told him.”

“Unless,” Philo added, “the man got in first and broke it after.”

“Then he broke it out of while he was in.”

“No,” said Philo. “He broke it into from the inside.”

Marshal Wittaker considered this.

“What we need,” he said finally, “is a fellow educated in them fine differences.”

Philo stood and buttoned his coat. He put Lesson Eleven in his pocket and selected a small notebook.

“We will examine the scene of the depredation,” he said.

Amos Griscom’s house stood on Elm Street, three doors beyond the Baptist church. A knot of citizens had already gathered at the gate. Among them was Billy Getz, the best-known practical joker in Riverbank.

Billy’s jokes were seldom cruel. They were merely frequent. He had once painted “Post No Bills” on every hitching post in town, and for a week no citizen had known whether the order applied to letters, advertisements, or William McKinley bank notes. He had also sent Marshal Wittaker a printed notice that the government intended to replace all town marshals with mounted cavalry.

Billy greeted Philo eagerly.

“Here comes Sherlock Gubb!” he cried. “Now we’ll catch—” He stopped and coughed. “I mean, now we’ll leave the catching entirely to you.”

Philo looked at him with narrow suspicion. Billy Getz had curly hair, bright eyes, and the expression of a boy who knew where the fireworks were hidden.

“Why did you commence to say ‘we’ll catch’?” Philo asked.

“I was going to say we’ll catch cold standing out here.”

“It is May.”

“I catch cold independent of seasons.”

Philo wrote in his notebook:

BILLY GETZ—SUSPICIOUS COLD IN MAY.

Mrs. Griscom met them in the parlor with the spoon wrapped in a handkerchief.

“I haven’t touched it since breakfast,” she said.

“You touched it to wrap it,” said Philo.

“I touched it before breakfast, then.”

“That changes the chronological docket but not the evidence.”

He examined the spoon. It was genuine silver, or at least looked sufficiently genuine to Mrs. Griscom. Philo smelled it, tapped it against his front tooth, measured it with a folding rule, and held it to the light.

“Has the criminal stole any spoons from elsewhere?” he asked.

“No,” said Mrs. Griscom. “He brought this one.”

Philo raised a solemn finger.

“A man can tie and he can untie. He can hitch and unhitch. He can buckle and unbuckle. Therefore, if he can burgle, he can un-burgle. This ain’t burglary. It is un-burglary.”

Billy Getz covered his mouth.

Marshal Wittaker coughed loudly.

Mrs. Griscom looked at the spoon.

“I don’t see why anybody would un-burgle us,” she said.

“That,” said Philo, “constitutes the motive.”

In the cellar he found the window open and one pane broken. Outside lay a chicken bone, two cigar ashes, and a crushed pansy. Philo collected the chicken bone in an envelope. He scraped the cigar ashes into another. He studied the pansy.

“The criminal trod here,” he said.

“So did Amos,” said Mrs. Griscom. “He fell into the flower bed when he came out to look.”

Philo examined Amos’s trousers. Purple stains marked both knees.

“That temporarily removes the pansy evidence from the criminal docket,” Philo said.

Billy Getz was leaning against the fence, smiling.

“What do you make of the chicken bone, Detective?” he asked.

“It came off a chicken.”

Billy’s smile weakened.

“How do you know?”

“The Rising Sun lesson on Bone Identification says a chicken bone can usually be identified by being the bone of a chicken.”

“You’ve got him there, Billy,” said Marshal Wittaker.

Philo returned to his shop convinced that Billy Getz was the un-burglar. Billy had been too interested. He had almost said, “We’ll catch—” and the chicken bone might have come from Billy’s dinner.

The next morning, however, Marshal Wittaker returned with news of a second un-burglary.

This time the victim was Attorney Medderbrook, who had discovered a silver spoon on his desk. It was engraved:

TO LUCIUS MEDDERBROOK  
AN ORNAMENT TO THE BAR

“Did the criminal enter through a cellar window?” Philo asked.

“He entered through the pantry,” said Wittaker. “Or un-entered. I ain’t got your education in this sort of crime.”

Philo inspected Medderbrook’s home. A pantry window had been pried open, a jar of pickles overturned, and a sack of flour disturbed. On the floor lay a long brass tube with a rubber bulb at one end.

Medderbrook, a short, stout man with a voice like water going down a narrow drain, gurgled indignantly.

“It is perfectly worthless!” he said.

“Utterly hopeless,” corrected his sister. “You always say perfectly worthless when you mean utterly hopeless.”

“I mean both!” Medderbrook gurgled. “A man enters my home, spills my pickles, scatters flour, and gives me a spoon! What sort of criminal is that?”

Philo lifted the brass tube.

“This may be a burglarious weapon.”

“It’s a lung tester,” said Billy Getz, who had arrived before the marshal. “You blow into it and the little pointer tells how much lung you’ve got.”

Philo placed the tube to his lips and blew.

A charge of flour shot from the other end and covered Billy’s face.

For a moment there was silence.

Then Marshal Wittaker sat down hard on a kitchen chair and laughed.

Billy wiped flour from his eyebrows.

“That’s a new model,” he said.

“I thought you claimed it was a lung tester,” Philo said.

“It tested your lungs.”

“It also tested your complexion,” said Wittaker.

Philo made another entry:

BILLY GETZ—FAMILIAR WITH CONCEALED FLOUR APPARATUS.

The Riverbank Eagle printed an account of the two crimes under the heading SILVER-SPOON FIEND AT LARGE. By noon, half the town was locking its windows, while the other half left windows open in the hope that the fiend might consider them prominent enough to receive silverware.

At two o’clock Mrs. Millbrook rushed into Philo’s shop. Mrs. Millbrook was round, breathless, and unable to speak without seeming to gurgle.

“He’s done it!” she gurgled.

“Who?” asked Philo.

“Him!”

“What?”

“It!”

“Where?”

“Our house!”

This cross-examination exhausted her, and she sat on the paste table until able to explain. Someone had entered the Millbrook residence during the family’s absence and left four engraved teaspoons in the dining room. The inscription read:

TO THE MILLBROOK FAMILY  
FOR SOCIAL MERIT

“Four!” cried Marshal Wittaker when he heard. “The fellow’s getting extravagant.”

“He is proceeding from retail to wholesale,” Philo said gravely. “Unless checked, he may ruin himself.”

That possibility genuinely concerned him. A criminal who stole was bad enough, but a criminal who gave away silver might eventually become a public charge.

At the Millbrook house, Philo discovered a muddy heel mark below the pantry window and another crushed flower bed. The flowers were yellow snapdragons. Yellow stains appeared on Billy Getz’s right trouser leg.

Philo’s heart beat faster.

“How come them stains?” he demanded.

Billy looked down.

“I fell into Mrs. Millbrook’s flowers when I heard she’d been un-burgled.”

“You also happened to be present at Griscom’s and Medderbrook’s.”

“I’m interested in crime.”

“You are interested previous to everybody else.”

“Maybe I read fast.”

Philo pointed an accusing finger.

“Mr. Getz, the deteckative eye is upon you.”

“Tell it not to wink,” Billy said.

Nevertheless, Philo was not satisfied. The Rising Sun course warned that the obvious suspect was seldom guilty unless he was, and that a detective should seek corroborative evidence by inductive, deductive, and seductive methods. The meaning of the third had not been explained, so Philo decided to employ the first two.

He spent the afternoon learning where silver spoons had recently been sold.

The jeweler had sold none of the engraved kind. The secondhand store had bought six from a riverboat cook and sold them to an elderly man who wore a black coat and kept his hat pulled low. The proprietor could not identify him because the man had paid cash, and cash, in the proprietor’s experience, made most customers look alike.

Philo considered elderly men in black coats.

Riverbank had twenty-seven.

Fourteen were eliminated because they did not have enough money to buy silver spoons. Eight were eliminated because they were ministers and would probably have delivered the spoons through the front door. Three were bedridden. One had gone to Davenport.

The remaining man was John Westcote.

John Westcote was the richest and stingiest citizen in Riverbank. He had once walked three blocks in the rain rather than pay a nickel for a streetcar. He owned houses, grain shares, mortgages, and enough unused collar buttons to supply the town. His eyesight was poor, his back was bent, and he moved with a tottering gait, but his reputation for meanness stood perfectly upright.

Philo went to Westcote’s house.

The old man opened the door three inches.

“What do you want?”

“Information in relation to silver spoons.”

“I haven’t any.”

“Did you purchase six?”

“No.”

“Did you not give Mr. and Mrs. Griscom a wedding present?”

“No.”

“Did you not give Attorney Medderbrook a wedding present?”

“He never married.”

“That saved you expense,” said Philo. “Did you give the Millbrooks a wedding present?”

“No.”

“When these various parties got married or became social ornaments, you neglected the customary bestowal of silver?”

“I neglect everything customary if it costs money.”

Philo’s eyes shone. Here was a motive of beautiful proportions.

John Westcote had grown old. His conscience, dormant for years, had awakened. Ashamed to confess publicly that he had failed to give wedding presents, he was secretly entering homes and depositing silverware. It was senile restitution, aggravated by remorse.

“Mr. Westcote,” Philo said kindly, “it ain’t too late to reform without breaking windows.”

Westcote slammed the door.

As Philo turned away, he noticed purple and yellow stains on the old man’s trousers.

The purple might have come from the Griscom pansies. The yellow might have come from the Millbrook snapdragons. Philo’s theory became almost painfully complete.

He hurried to Marshal Wittaker’s office. Billy Getz was there, sitting with his feet on the stove.

“The case is practically solved,” Philo announced.

Billy dropped his feet.

“Not already!”

“I have located the guilty conscience.”

“You mean the guilty party?”

“The party and conscience are combined in John Westcote.”

Marshal Wittaker stared.

“Old Westcote? He wouldn’t give away a bent pin.”

“Exactly,” said Philo. “He has been withholding wedding presents for forty years. His internal remorse has fermented. He is now paying them under cover of darkness.”

Billy swallowed a laugh.

“Philo,” he said, “that’s wonderful.”

“It is inductive.”

“It is more than that.”

“Do you know anything about it?”

“Me? No. Nothing whatever.” Billy rose. “And if I were you, I’d shadow Westcote tonight. He may be planning a big delivery.”

Philo looked sharply at him.

“Why should you suggest that?”

“Professional admiration.”

The false mustaches in Philo’s pocket seemed suddenly heavy. He had brought them in accordance with Lesson Eleven. Billy Getz was urging him to follow Westcote because Billy expected him to look foolish. That was evident. It was also evident that Billy knew more than he admitted.

Philo therefore decided to follow Westcote.

He selected a black mustache, although he already had one of his own, because the lesson said a disguise altered a man’s appearance. He pasted the false mustache above his natural mustache, put on blue spectacles, turned his coat inside out, and went to wait behind the hedge opposite Westcote’s house.

At seven-thirty, John Westcote came out carrying a newspaper-wrapped bundle.

Philo’s confidence rose.

The old man looked up and down the street, then set off toward the eastern end of town. Philo followed according to correspondence-school rules: twenty paces behind on open streets, ten paces behind in crowds, and out of sight whenever the suspect looked backward.

There were no crowds. There was only Mrs. Purdy’s goat, which followed Philo because it liked the taste of the lining of his reversed coat.

Westcote turned.

Philo stepped behind a maple tree. The goat remained visible, chewing his coattail.

Westcote continued.

Philo continued, dragging the goat until the lining tore. He abandoned the reversed-coat portion of the disguise and followed in his shirtsleeves.

The old man passed the gasworks, crossed the creek bridge, and entered the hazel brush beyond the town limits. Here he stopped beside a stump, set down the newspaper bundle, and moved away rapidly.

Philo waited.

Two men emerged from the brush. They did not resemble persons collecting neglected wedding presents. One was broad and heavy, with a cap pulled over his eyes. The other had a narrow face and a scar across his cheek. The broad man picked up the bundle.

“Count it,” said the narrow one.

The pair moved deeper into the brush.

Philo followed.

The men sat behind a fallen tree and opened the package. Inside were bank notes, which the broad man counted by the light of a shaded lantern.

“One thousand,” he said.

“He paid, then.”

“He’d pay twice that rather than have his mills touched.”

“He’ll pay again.”

The narrow-faced man laughed.

“After the Derlingport crusher job, these old moneybags know we mean business. We’ll send him another letter next week. If he squeals, we’ll put enough powder under his lumber mill to scatter boards from here to Missouri.”

Philo crouched behind a hazel bush, hardly breathing.

The Derlingport stone crusher!

These were not un-burglars. They were dynamiters—wholesale criminals of the five-thousand-dollar variety.

His original reasoning had not been wrong, Philo told himself. It had merely arrived at a different crime than the one it had started toward.

The men wrapped the money again and moved off through the brush. Philo followed. The route led behind Westcote’s lumberyard, across a vacant lot, and into the railway yards. A freight train stood on a siding, its locomotive breathing patiently in the darkness.

The men approached an empty boxcar.

A voice from within said, “That you, Jake?”

“It’s us.”

“Got the cash?”

“All of it.”

The two climbed into the car.

Philo crept near and placed his ear against the wooden side. Through a crack he saw three men seated on nail kegs. One held the lantern. Another had a revolver across his knees.

“He paid easy,” said Jake.

“He’ll pay easier next time,” said the man with the revolver. “We’ll hit the grain elevator if he don’t.”

“What about the other three?”

“They’re waiting near Blandon. We meet them tomorrow. Then we split the money and make for Chicago.”

“How soon does this car move?”

“Any minute.”

Philo withdrew his ear.

There were five men in the car, three accomplices near Blandon, and a freight train about to move. The usual detective might have summoned help. Philo was not near any help. He might have entered the car and arrested the men, but five dynamiters and one revolver presented an unfavorable retail proportion.

He examined the boxcar door.

It slid on an iron track. A hasp hung beside it. The men had left the door open for air.

Philo removed his shoes, because Lesson Eleven stated that rubber-soled footwear was best for silent work and stockings were second best. He crept forward, seized the door, and slid it shut.

A shout came from inside.

Philo dropped the hasp and thrust his steel paper-hanger’s scraper through it in place of a padlock.

The door shook.

“Who’s there?”

Philo looked about. The train jerked.

The boxcar began to move.

Philo had intended to remain behind and notify Marshal Wittaker by telephone. Unfortunately, his scraper was his best tool, and the shaking door threatened to work it loose. He seized the ladder on the end of the car and climbed.

The train gathered speed.

Inside, the dynamiters hammered at the door and used language not included in the Rising Sun course.

Philo clung to the ladder as the railway yards slid past. The lights of Riverbank vanished. Wind pulled at his false mustache, and presently it departed into the night. His natural mustache remained, proving its superior attachment.

At the first grade crossing, Philo shouted to the watchman, but the watchman thought he was a tramp and advised him to get off. At the second crossing there was no watchman. At the third, the train was moving too fast for conversation.

The door continued to shake.

Philo climbed to the roof, crawled forward over three cars, and reached the caboose. The conductor discovered him entering through the rear door without shoes.

“Where did you come from?” the conductor demanded.

“Riverbank.”

“Where are your shoes?”

“Following a separate deteckative career.”

Philo explained.

The conductor did not believe him until they walked forward along the train at the next stop and heard the prisoners threatening to blow up the entire railway if they were not released.

“That sounds like dynamiters,” the conductor admitted.

At the town of Cresswell, the conductor telegraphed the sheriff. Twelve armed men surrounded the car. The scraper was removed, the door was opened, and the five prisoners were invited to emerge with their hands high.

They emerged.

By noon the next day, one had confessed. By evening, the three accomplices near Blandon had been arrested. A telegram was sent to Riverbank, but Philo remained in Cresswell to identify the men and to make a statement twelve pages long, including his theory concerning senile wedding restitution.

Meanwhile, Riverbank experienced another un-burglary.

Judge Purcell returned from court to discover a silver soup ladle in his piano. It was engraved:

TO JUDGE PURCELL  
HOPING TO BE NOTICED

The judge was not pleased. He organized the marshal, two deputies, Amos Griscom, and a night watchman into a trap.

That night they hid inside the home of Mayor Higby, whose prominence made him a likely recipient. At eleven-fifteen, a cellar window opened. A thin, shabby young man crawled through, carrying a package.

He tiptoed into the dining room, unwrapped a silver gravy boat, and set it on the table.

Marshal Wittaker lit the lamp.

“Hold on there!”

The young man threw up his hands and smiled.

“Is this the party?” he asked.

“What party?”

“The party you’re going to invite me to.”

No one knew his name at first. He was a harmless, simple-minded fellow who slept in an abandoned shed near the river and earned occasional pennies carrying parcels. He explained that he had dreamed prominent families were giving dinners. In the dream, anyone who presented them with silverware was invited.

“I gave them spoons,” he said, “so they’d know I was sociable.”

“Where’d you get the silver?” asked Wittaker.

“Found money in an old boot under the shed.”

It was later learned that the money had belonged to a tramp imprisoned in Davenport. The silver had been purchased honestly, the engraving paid for honestly, and the entering of houses done with no intention beyond establishing social relations.

“You could have knocked at the doors,” Marshal Wittaker said.

“They might’ve said no.”

“That’s so,” Billy Getz admitted. “Riverbank society is particular.”

The young man was given supper and placed under the care of the county. Thus the un-burglary case ended without the aid of Philo Gubb.

Billy was in Marshal Wittaker’s office the next morning when the telegram arrived.

Wittaker opened it and read:

HAVE FIVE DERLINGPORT DYNAMITERS IN CUSTODY. THREE MORE TAKEN AT BLANDON ON CONFESSION. PHILO GUBB RESPONSIBLE FOR CAPTURE. REWARD FIVE THOUSAND PAYABLE ACCORDING TO TERMS. EXPECT HIM HOME THURSDAY.

Marshal Wittaker read it twice.

Billy took the telegram and read it once.

“He caught them?” Billy asked faintly.

“Five in a boxcar.”

“And three more?”

“On confession.”

“And the reward?”

“Five thousand.”

Billy sat down.

The room was very quiet.

At last Marshal Wittaker said, “You got him started on Westcote.”

“I did.”

“You stained your trousers in them flower beds on purpose.”

“I did.”

“You put the flour-shooter in Medderbrook’s pantry.”

Billy sighed.

“I did. I heard about the first spoon, and I thought it would be funny to add some clues and watch Philo investigate. Old Westcote really did fall into both flower beds because I told him somebody had dropped a dime in each one. I figured Philo would follow him all night and look foolish.”

“He followed him.”

“Yes.”

“And caught eight dynamiters.”

“Yes.”

Marshal Wittaker leaned back and stared at the ceiling.

“It don’t seem right,” he said.

“No.”

“He was wrong about you.”

“Yes.”

“He was wrong about Westcote giving wedding presents.”

“Yes.”

“He was wrong about the spoons.”

“Yes.”

“He was wrong all the way through.”

“Entirely.”

“And he gets five thousand dollars.”

Billy folded the telegram carefully and handed it back.

“How much does he still owe on Syrilla?” he asked.

“Seven hundred and something.”

“So he can marry her.”

“Looks that way.”

“And have over four thousand left.”

“Looks that way.”

Billy rose and put on his hat.

“I feel bilious,” he said.

Marshal Wittaker nodded.

“I feel worse than that.”

“What do you feel?”

“Utterly hopeless.”

Billy paused at the door.

“You mean perfectly worthless.”

“I mean both,” said Marshal Wittaker.

## The Cartographer of Lost Hours

Every morning at six, Mara Venn unlocked the brass door beneath the eastern clock tower and went to work mapping the previous day.

Her office had no windows. The city had decided long ago that windows encouraged inaccuracy in civil servants, particularly those whose duties involved time. Instead, a hundred glass cabinets lined the walls, each containing clocks that had stopped for reasons no watchmaker could explain.

One showed thirteen minutes past midnight, though midnight had never arrived on the date engraved beneath it. Another ran backward whenever someone lied nearby. The oldest clock had no hands at all. It ticked only during thunderstorms.

At the center of the room stood Mara’s desk. On it lay a blank map, a silver compass, and the official ledger of missing hours.

The city of Bellwether lost time in small quantities. Seven minutes might vanish from a bakery between the kneading of dough and the lighting of ovens. A schoolroom might misplace an entire afternoon. Now and then, a citizen would leave home on Monday and reach the market on Wednesday, convinced the journey had taken half an hour.

These losses were rarely dangerous. Time, like rainwater, found cracks.

Mara’s task was to locate those cracks, measure them, and draw them on the municipal maps in violet ink. The city council used her work to determine where new clocks should be built and which streets required warning signs.

CAUTION: TUESDAYS UNSTABLE.

DO NOT LINGER AFTER THE NINTH BELL.

SENIOR CITIZENS MAY EXPERIENCE YOUTH.

Mara had been the city’s cartographer of lost hours for eleven years. She was precise, patient, and entirely alone.

At eight minutes after six on the first day of winter, a boy appeared inside the office.

He did not enter through the door. One moment Mara was drawing the outline of a missing quarter-hour near Weaver’s Square; the next, he was standing beside Cabinet Forty-Three, dripping rain onto the tiled floor.

He was perhaps twelve years old. His coat was too large, his boots were tied with string, and in his arms he carried a black wooden box.

“You’re late,” he said.

Mara looked at the locked door, then at the boy.

“For what?”

“For finding me.”

He set the box on her desk.

Mara reached for the alarm bell beneath the ledger, but the boy placed one hand over it.

“If you call the guards, I’ll disappear again.”

“That sounds like their problem.”

“It becomes yours in three days.”

His voice was calm, but his fingers trembled.

Mara studied him more carefully. There was a bruise on his cheek, yellow at the edges as if it were several days old. His wet hair clung to his forehead. Around his neck hung a copper disk stamped with the emblem of the city: a bell inside a circle.

“Who are you?”

“My name is Eli.”

“Family name?”

“I don’t know yet.”

Mara had heard many strange answers in that room, but never that one.

“What’s in the box?”

“You should open it.”

“I should do no such thing.”

“You already did.”

Eli lifted the lid.

Inside lay a pocket watch.

Its case was badly scratched, and its chain had been broken. The watch’s single hand spun so quickly that it was only a silver blur. Engraved inside the lid were the words:

TO MARA, WHO ALWAYS FINDS THE WAY BACK.

Mara’s breath caught.

She knew the handwriting.

Her father had written those words on the morning of her tenth birthday, forty years ago.

The watch had vanished with him the following winter.

She picked it up. It was warm.

“Where did you get this?”

“You gave it to me.”

“I’ve never seen you before.”

“You will.”

Mara closed the lid and put the watch down with deliberate care.

“My father disappeared with this watch. The inspectors searched every unstable district in the city. They found nothing.”

“They were looking in the wrong year.”

Something clicked in Cabinet Twelve. A clock began striking, though it had no bell.

Mara stared at Eli.

There were approved ways to discuss temporal displacement. There were forms, definitions, and legal distinctions. A person could be delayed, repeated, reversed, or mislaid. The dead, however, remained dead. The Department of Hours was emphatic on that point.

“My father died,” she said.

“No,” Eli replied. “He got lost.”

“Where?”

“In the day after tomorrow.”

The clock in Cabinet Twelve stopped.

Eli swayed. Mara caught him before his head struck the desk.

He weighed almost nothing.

She carried him to the narrow bench by the wall and wrapped him in her spare coat. When she turned back, the black box was gone.

The pocket watch remained.

By seven, Eli was still asleep. By eight, three municipal messengers had knocked on the brass door. Mara ignored them. At half past nine, the chief inspector arrived with a key of his own.

Orrin Vale filled the doorway like a badly built cupboard. He wore a gray uniform fastened to the chin and carried a stack of blue warrants under one arm.

“You failed to submit yesterday’s map,” he said.

“I’m revising it.”

“You’ve never revised anything.”

“There’s a first time for all disasters.”

Vale stepped inside. His eyes moved to the sleeping boy.

“Who is that?”

“My assistant.”

“Your assistant is sixty-three and has a mustache.”

“I replaced him.”

“With a child?”

“He works cheaply.”

Vale approached the bench. Mara stood between them.

The chief inspector frowned. “Where did he come from?”

“North district.”

“Which street?”

“I didn’t ask.”

“You ask everyone.”

“Perhaps I’m becoming careless.”

“Then perhaps you’re becoming unemployed.”

Behind him, the clocks in the cabinets began ticking together.

It was a sound Mara had heard only once before, during the collapse of the old observatory. A hundred mechanisms found the same rhythm, and the room seemed to tighten around it.

Tick.

Tick.

Tick.

Vale glanced at the cabinets.

“Is that normal?”

“Perfectly.”

Tick.

Tick.

The pocket watch on Mara’s desk sprang open.

Its spinning hand stopped.

It pointed not to a number, but toward Vale.

The inspector’s face changed.

He moved quickly for a large man. One hand seized the watch while the other struck Mara across the mouth. She fell against the desk, scattering pens and rulers.

Vale turned toward the door.

Eli sat up.

“Don’t let him take it,” he said.

Mara grabbed the silver compass and hurled it.

It struck Vale’s wrist. He cursed and dropped the watch. The moment it touched the floor, the office vanished.

Mara landed on wet cobblestones beneath a violet sky.

Rain hung motionless in the air. Each drop was a clear bead, suspended between cloud and street. A horse stood frozen beside an overturned carriage. Flames leaned from the windows of a nearby house but gave no heat. Above the rooftops, the eastern clock tower bent at an impossible angle, its bells scattered upward like birds.

Eli lay beside her.

Vale was nowhere in sight.

Mara touched the blood on her lip.

“What happened?”

“The watch opened a door,” Eli said.

“To where?”

He pointed down the street.

A newspaper floated above the pavement, caught in a wind that had stopped. Mara plucked it from the air.

The date was two days ahead.

The headline read:

CATASTROPHIC TIME FAILURE  
EASTERN DISTRICT LOST  
THOUSANDS MISSING

Below it was a photograph of the clock tower collapsing into a black circle in the sky.

“This is the day after tomorrow,” Mara whispered.

“Part of it.”

“Where are the people?”

“Between seconds.”

“Why aren’t we?”

“The watch keeps us moving.”

Mara looked at the pocket watch in her hand. Its silver hand now turned slowly, one revolution every few breaths.

“Where is Vale?”

“He has his own way through.”

“You know him?”

Eli nodded. “He caused this.”

They followed the frozen street toward the clock tower. As they walked, Mara saw the city caught at the instant of disaster. A woman knelt beside a fallen basket, reaching for apples suspended above the gutter. Two children hovered in mid-jump over a rope. A flock of pigeons filled the square like gray stars.

At the entrance to the tower, a crack divided the air.

It was thin as thread and blacker than darkness. Through it, Mara glimpsed other versions of the square: one buried in snow, one flooded to the rooftops, one crowded with people wearing fashions from a century before.

She had mapped thousands of temporal fractures, but always from the safe side. This one did not feel like a gap in time. It felt like a wound.

“The city can’t survive a break this large,” she said.

“It doesn’t.”

“How do we stop it?”

“We find your father.”

The tower doors were gone. Beyond them, the staircase spiraled upward through the hollow center of the building.

Mara began to climb.

As a child, she had spent every Sunday inside that tower. Her father, Jon Venn, had been keeper of the eastern clock, and he had allowed her to polish the gears while he adjusted the great brass pendulum.

He believed clocks were not machines for measuring time. They were promises.

“Every tick says the next moment is coming,” he once told her. “Every tock says it arrived.”

Then, one winter morning, he had gone to repair a fault in the tower and never returned.

Mara had waited beneath the clock until nightfall. Afterward, she had spent years learning the shape of time’s cracks, convinced that knowledge could prevent anyone else from being lost.

Now she climbed with her father’s watch beating in her palm.

At the seventh landing, they found a door that had never been there before.

Eli opened it.

On the other side was a summer afternoon from forty years ago.

Sunlight entered through the tower windows. The gears turned. Ten-year-old Mara sat cross-legged on the floor, eating sugared plums from a paper bag.

Her father stood at the workbench, engraving a pocket watch.

Mara stopped in the doorway.

She remembered this day: the smell of oil, the sticky sweetness on her fingers, the golden dust in the air. She remembered her father’s rolled sleeves and the tune he whistled when he was concentrating.

Young Mara looked up.

“Papa,” she said, “there’s a lady at the door.”

Jon Venn turned.

For one reckless moment, Mara wanted to run to him. She wanted to say everything at once: that she had waited, that she had searched, that she had spent forty years angry with him for being dead.

But Eli pulled her backward.

“This isn’t him,” the boy said. “It’s only an hour he left behind.”

The summer room flickered.

Jon smiled politely at them, unaware that he was a memory.

“Can I help you?” he asked.

Mara could not answer.

The scene repeated.

Young Mara ate a sugared plum. Jon engraved the watch. Dust turned in the sunlight.

“Papa, there’s a lady at the door.”

They closed it.

On the ninth landing, they found Vale.

He stood before the central mechanism, where the tower’s great pendulum should have been. In its place spun a sphere of black glass. Threads of violet light stretched from the sphere into the walls, trembling with each distant tick.

Vale held the other end of the pocket watch’s broken chain.

“I wondered when you would catch up,” he said.

Mara stepped in front of Eli.

“What is that thing?”

“A reservoir.”

“For stolen time?”

“Recovered time,” Vale corrected. “Do you know how much the city wastes? Hours spent sleeping. Years lost to illness. Whole lifetimes squandered by people who have no idea what to do with them.”

“You caused the fractures.”

“I collected what leaked through them.”

“For what purpose?”

Vale placed his hand against the black sphere.

The glass cleared.

Inside it, a young woman lay in a white bed. Her dark hair spread across the pillow, and a bouquet of dried flowers rested beside her. She was perfectly still.

“My daughter, Lysa,” Vale said. “She died seventeen years ago.”

Mara looked at him. “You can’t bring back the dead.”

“No. But I can return to a time when she was alive.”

“You’re destroying the city.”

“A city is stone. Stone can be rebuilt.”

“There are people frozen in the streets.”

“Then they’ll never suffer. That’s more mercy than time showed my child.”

His fingers tightened around the chain.

The pocket watch tore from Mara’s hand and flew toward him.

Eli lunged for it.

Vale caught the boy by the coat and dragged him close.

For the first time, the inspector looked afraid.

“You,” he whispered.

Eli struggled, but Vale held him fast.

Mara took one step forward.

“Let him go.”

“Do you know what he is?” Vale asked. “He isn’t a child. He’s a consequence.”

The black sphere brightened. Within it, the image of Vale’s daughter faded, replaced by a web of streets and clocks. Violet lines converged on Eli’s heart.

“When the eastern district collapses,” Vale said, “all its possible futures collapse with it. Every life that might have been lived becomes energy. The boy is one of those lives. He slipped out before the failure was complete.”

Mara stared at Eli.

“What does that mean?”

The boy’s eyes filled with tears, though his voice remained steady.

“My name is Eli Venn.”

The tower groaned.

“Venn?” Mara said.

“You’re my grandmother.”

For a moment, the fractured tower, the ruined city, and Vale’s machine all became very far away.

“I have no children.”

“Not yet.”

“Then your mother—”

“Isn’t born yet. She won’t be if the city ends today.”

Mara understood his first answer then.

He did not know his full history because it had not happened. He was a branch growing from a tree not yet planted.

Vale pulled him toward the sphere.

“That’s why he can repair it,” he said. “An unlived lifetime is enough to stabilize the reservoir.”

“You mean kill him.”

“He was never born.”

“He’s here.”

“That is not the same.”

“It is to him.”

Mara moved.

She seized the loose chain and wrapped it around her wrist. Vale jerked backward. The pocket watch swung between them, opening and closing as if gasping for breath.

The sphere pulsed.

For an instant Mara saw dozens of rooms inside it: hospital rooms, nurseries, kitchens, graves. She saw Vale holding his dying daughter’s hand. She saw Eli as a baby in someone’s arms. She saw herself older, laughing at a table surrounded by people whose names she did not know.

Then the chain snapped.

Mara fell against the mechanism.

The world rang.

Not the tower bell. Not any sound made by metal or air. It was the noise of a thousand lost hours returning at once.

The sphere cracked.

Vale screamed and reached for it.

“Lysa!”

A hand appeared inside the glass.

The young woman was awake now. She sat upright in the white bed and looked through the sphere at her father.

Vale pressed both palms to the surface.

“I’m coming,” he said.

Lysa shook her head.

Even through the glass, Mara saw the sadness in her face.

She formed one word with her lips.

Live.

Then the sphere shattered.

Time poured out.

The staircase buckled. Rain crashed against the windows. Bells fell through the tower, striking stone and wood. Somewhere below, the city resumed its unfinished second: horses cried out, people shouted, glass broke, and thunder rolled across the roofs.

A wave of violet light lifted Eli from the floor.

Mara caught his hand.

He was already becoming transparent.

“Hold on!”

“I can’t.”

“Yes, you can.”

“You have to find him,” Eli said.

“Who?”

“Your father. He’s in the last room.”

Another wave passed through him. Mara could see the gears through his chest.

“Will I see you again?” she asked.

Eli smiled.

“You already did.”

His hand vanished from hers.

The tower lurched. Vale lay beside the ruined sphere, alive but unmoving.

Mara wanted to stay. She wanted to search the air for any trace of Eli. But the floor split beneath her, and beyond it she saw a final staircase leading upward.

She climbed.

At the top of the tower was a small circular room.

Her father sat beneath the bell.

He was older than she remembered. His hair was white, his face thin, his workman’s coat patched at both elbows. Around him lay thousands of maps drawn in violet ink.

Jon Venn looked up and smiled.

“You took your time,” he said.

Mara stood in the doorway, unable to breathe.

He rose slowly.

“I tried to get back,” he continued. “But the fracture carried me forward. I arrived here two days after I left, except the two days were forty years apart.”

“You were alive.”

“Yes.”

“All this time?”

“Not from where I was sitting.”

She crossed the room and struck him in the chest.

He accepted the blow.

She struck him again, then clutched his coat and pressed her face against his shoulder.

“I waited,” she said.

“I know.”

“You left me.”

“I know.”

“I thought you were dead.”

“I’m sorry.”

He held her while the tower shook.

After a while, Mara stepped back.

“Eli said you could stop this.”

“Not me.” Jon pointed to the maps. “You.”

The drawings covered every year of the city’s history. They showed fractures Mara had mapped herself, as well as thousands she had never seen. Together they formed a single vast pattern.

A clock face.

At its center was the eastern tower.

“The missing hours were never random,” Jon said. “They’re pieces of one mechanism. Vale tried to wind it backward. You must let it move forward.”

“How?”

“Complete the map.”

He handed her a violet pen.

One section remained blank: a narrow curve through the city’s eastern district. Mara recognized it as the path she had walked with Eli through the frozen rain.

She drew the line.

Below them, every clock in Bellwether struck at once.

The sound traveled through streets and houses, through kitchens, schools, hospitals, and graves. Lost minutes slipped beneath doors. Mislaid afternoons fell from rooftops. Forgotten birthdays returned in flashes of candlelight. Citizens woke with sudden memories of conversations they had never finished.

The great bell above Mara swung.

The tower became transparent.

For one heartbeat she saw the whole city not as stone, but as a living map of moments: every beginning, every ending, every choice opening into another.

Among them stood Eli.

He raised one hand.

Then the bell struck, and the vision disappeared.

Mara woke on the floor of her office.

Morning light did not enter, because the room still had no windows. Yet she knew it was morning from the ordinary, comforting disorder of the clocks. Some ticked. Some did not. One chimed whenever dust settled on its case.

The pocket watch lay beside her.

Its hand moved normally.

On the bench sat her father, asleep beneath her spare coat.

Chief Inspector Vale was found that afternoon in the eastern tower. He confessed to seventeen years of unauthorized experiments and was sentenced to spend the remainder of his career repairing every public clock he had damaged. He accepted the judgment without protest.

Once a year, on the anniversary of his daughter’s death, he stopped all the clocks in his workshop for one hour.

Then he started them again.

The city council denied that any catastrophe had occurred. Governments preferred disasters that left rubble. Nevertheless, new signs appeared throughout the eastern district:

CAUTION: FUTURE UNDER CONSTRUCTION.

Mara continued mapping lost hours, though she no longer worked alone. Jon took the desk beside hers and complained daily about modern pens. Together they redrew the municipal charts, adding not only the places where time had broken, but also the places where it had healed.

Years passed.

Mara married late, surprising everyone, especially herself. She had a daughter who grew up fascinated by bells and entirely uninterested in maps. The girl traveled beyond the city, returned with stories, and eventually brought home a quiet musician with wet boots and kind eyes.

On the first day of winter, many years after the tower nearly fell, Mara was summoned from her office by a note written in her daughter’s hurried hand.

She arrived at the hospital shortly after dawn.

Her daughter lay exhausted but smiling beneath white sheets. In her arms was a small boy with dark hair.

“Would you like to hold him?” she asked.

Mara took the child carefully.

He opened his eyes.

Around his neck, her daughter had tied a copper disk stamped with the emblem of the city: a bell inside a circle.

“We haven’t chosen a family name,” the musician said, “but we thought Eli for his first.”

The baby wrapped his hand around Mara’s finger.

From far across Bellwether came the sound of the eastern clock striking six. Every promise in the city answered: tick and tock, loss and return, the next moment coming and the next moment arrived.

Mara held her grandson close.

“You’re late,” Eli said.

Or perhaps it was only the clock.
